docs/alphaconversion.html.summary: Alpha Project Conversion Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson If your project existed before 2026/the release of the Beta, please follow these steps to reduce the destruction of data in your project, as a majority of data was changed and therefore will likely need to be redone in order to work with the new architecture, usually the case with UI. We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause. Please stay up to date either in the discord or our social media in the event this information is/needs to be updated! Converting Alpha code to Beta Convert your Unity Version by simply opening it with a different version through unity hub. Say yes to all conversion popups unity mentions. If they are sending errors, remove the serialized fields from ISaveManager & ISaveable. Remove Text mesh pro's examples and extras scripts Re-import TMP by: Window/Text Mesh Pro/Import TMP Essentials. Remove previous DREditor through file explorer Add new DREditor (preferably through file explorer as well but the UPM should work.) Let it compile, then fix any errors on your project specific scripts. (if applicable) If the dependency window shows up follow it's instructions. If they are present in your assets folder delete the DOTween folder and the CharTweener folder. Tools/DREditor/Dependencies/Reset Dependencies Go through the dependency set up process. Commit changes to github. Convert all Room Data In any scene, place the Room_State_Manager prefab. Hit the drop down and select Actor. Fill it in with your Character Database, the list field below it should populate. Rename it to Room_State_Manager_YOURPROJECTACRONYM Example: Room_State_Manager_EG Drag your now named prefab into the project window. Turn it into a prefab variant. Commit changes to github. Tools/Convert/Convert All Room Data Builders Commit changes to github. Tools/Convert/Convert Scene Room Managers Fill in the field with your newly made Room_State_Manager_YOURPROJECTACRONYM Press the button below. Commit changes to github. Convert Doors Tools/Scriptable Object Assigner Under Components just put the Door script. Under Scriptable Objects put these: InLeaveProcess HasMenuAccess CurrentControlsKey CheckOverlay OnFinishedLoadingRoom ChangingObserve InMenu IsLoadingToRoom InDialogue Press "Assign to All Components in Scenes" Actors Select all actor prefab variants. Click Tools/Convert/Actors/Update Selected Actor Display Names. Select all actor prefab variants again. Click Tools/Convert/Actors/Update Selected Actor Colliders. Convert Triggers ONLY DO AFTER ALL ROOM DATA IS CONVERTED: Tools/Convert/Triggers/Convert All Trigger Assets. AFTER ALL TRIGGERS CONVERTED CHECK ALL OF THEM to ensure subsequents are actually the class that they are, as there has been an instance where a dialogue subsequent had it's type name correct but it's class was converted to a move player subsequent. If you find this to be the case and need help contact Sweden for support. Convert Custom Dialogue Events Tools/Convert/Replace Asset Text Editor The lookfor and replacewith fields should already have what's necessary: "ns: , asm: Assembly-CSharp" & "ns: DREditor.CustomEvents, asm: DREditor.CustomEvents" So just click Convert. Convert Dialogue Events Tools/Convert/Replace Asset Text Editor Click Update Reworked Dialogue Events. Convert Animation Events Tools/Convert/Replace Asset Text Editor Look For: class: AnimationEvent, ns: , asm: DREditor Replace With: class: AnimationEvent, ns: DREditor.Dialogues.Events, asm: DREditor Fixing CamToPosition Dialogue Events All CamToPosition Events on existing dialogues will be broken, to fix this: Select your dialogue asset with this issue, hit ctrl + s to save. Go to your Github Desktop/source control. There should be a change for your asset. Select it to view what was changed on the asset and scroll all the way down. You should see "objectName:" some where, whatever the object name is, will be what you have to re-input into the CamToPosition Event. Additional Notices Notice that Dialogue Events in SaveableStateData Assets may be broken, and while this is highly unlikely, if you find this to be the case please contact Sweden for additional support. There is a possibility that All Flash screen White events and original ActorFade/line.Leave bools will be removed and need to be re-applied manually. If you learn this to be the case please contact sweden for support.

docs/codingguidelines.html.title: Coding Guidelines | DREditor API
docs/codingguidelines.html.summary: Coding Guidelines Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson ALERT: Note that maintainers reserve the right to deny any request regardless of these rules being followed. ALERT: Please do not submit hundreds of requests for "optimization" reasons unless you can present tangible evidence of an impact the project maintainers deem reasonable. Do not request changes just because it's "technically faster". REPORT: Requests for changes that involve the unity addressables require maintainer level permission at minimum but will likely be denied. Reason being that it would be asinine to expect non programmers to keep track of and attempt to understand the addressables system. In order to maintain quality and to enforce easy readability for both programmers and non programmers, all non-third party code files must adhere to these rules. If you attempt to contribute code not following these rules, your request will be denied. "Programmers should not want to blow their head off reading the code". "Someone who does not know how to code, should be able to reasonably piece together what your code does". Code must be in the proper namespace based on where it's intended to be located. Everything that can, must have XML summaries. (they don't need to be filled out though, the community can do that if they wish) All fields visible in the inspector must have tooltips. (they must match the XML summaries) The xml /// tag must be used on things like overridden functions and interface implementations. You do not have to follow this rule if you write out the xml summary yourself instead. If your script is a monobehaviour that is not abstract, you must use a ClassHeader attribute and use the nameof keyword to list out what the script inherits. Code must do their best to follow Uncle Bobs Guide to Clean Code. Code must do their best to follow NDepend Rules. However, there are some caveats. Logs must do their best to follow Log Designations. Author your code at the top with //Author: how you want to be credited You must separate lines of code by a new line, 2 lines to separate between fields and functions. This is also done to separate functions implemented from interfaces. Unless a valid reason is given, all properties and functions should be virtual with protected or public. This is to allow easier extensions. An example of a valid script can be seen below. //Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson : Discord: sweden_gaming For Project Eden's Garden using DREditor.FreeTimeSurfacing; using DREditor.ItemRolling; using DREditor.Processables; using DREditor.Utility; using UnityEngine; namespace DREditor.GachaSurface { /// <summary> /// Summary of the class /// </summary> [ClassHeader(nameof(SubmittableFTESurfaceCollection) + ", " + nameof(SubmittableFTESurfaceComponent) + ", " + nameof(FTESurfaceComponent) + ", " + nameof(ISubmittable) + ", " + nameof(IComponentsCache) + ", " + nameof(IRollerContainer) + "\n\nText Matching XML")] public class Gacha : SubmittableFTESurfaceCollection, IRollerContainer { /// <summary> /// Summary of what the field is/what it's for etc. /// </summary> [Header(nameof(Gacha) + " Fields")] [Divider] [Tooltip("Text Matching XML")] [SerializeField] protected ItemRollerBase roller; /// <inheritdoc/> public virtual IItemRoller GetRoller() => roller; /// <inheritdoc/> protected override void OnSubmit() { RollItem(); ProcessRollResult(); } /// <summary> /// /// </summary> protected virtual void RollItem() => roller.RollForItem(); /// <summary> /// /// </summary> protected virtual void ProcessRollResult() { if (RollSucceded()) OnRollSucceded(); else OnRollFailed(); } /// <summary> /// /// </summary> /// <returns></returns> protected virtual bool RollSucceded() => roller.TryGetRolledObject(out object _); /// <summary> /// /// </summary> protected virtual void OnRollSucceded() { this.InvokeThisPlusComponents<IItemRollerResponse>((response) => response?.InitializeForResponse(roller)); base.OnSubmit(); } /// <summary> /// /// </summary> protected virtual void OnRollFailed() { AlertRollFailed(); base.InvokeCompleted(); } /// <summary> /// /// </summary> protected virtual void AlertRollFailed() => UnityEngine.Debug.LogWarning($"ALERT: The item roller failed in rolling an item! Forcing process as Complete."); /// <summary> /// Tells the roller to give the rolled item before completing the gacha process. /// </summary> protected override void InvokeCompleted() { roller.GivePlayerRolledItem(); base.InvokeCompleted(); } } }

docs/contributing.html.title: Contributing to DREditor | DREditor API
docs/contributing.html.summary: Contributing to DREditor Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Thank you for your interest in contributing to DREditor! We value community contributions and appreciate your help in making DREditor better. Please note that this information may be subject to change in the future! Types of Contributions We Accept ✅ We Encourage and Accept Bug fixes and patches: If you've found a bug and have a fix, we welcome your contribution. Security vulnerability reports: Please report security issues responsibly by contacting the project maintainer. Documentation improvements: Help make our docs clearer and more comprehensive. Testing and feedback: Report issues, test new features, and provide feedback. Small code improvements: Performance optimizations, code cleanup, and minor enhancements ⚠️ Discuss First Feature requests & Large changes: Please open a request on the discord or contact the project maintainer. As we must ensure that requests and large changes will be overall worth the time spent into them. As we must ensure bug testing as to not obstruct active users development with their projects using DREditor. If your change or feature does not edit any actual code within the repository, consider making it a community plugin! We're happy to assist those wishing to do so. ❌ Generally Not Accepted Reworks of existing Code: If it isn't broken don't fix it. Please leave reworks to the project maintainer or at least request it so the project maintainer can take care of it. Large external feature contributions: Features carry a long-term maintenance burden. To reduce burnout and maintain code quality, we typically implement major features internally. This allows us to ensure consistency with the overall architecture and maintain the high reliability that DREditor users depend on. Breaking changes: Changes that break backward compatibility require extensive discussion and depending on the circumstance will likely not be accepted. Code that does not follow NDepend Rules: In order to remove overall technical debt. The Project Maintainer Sweden has spent his own money on the technical software NDepend which helps maintain code health. You as a contributor are not required to have NDepend, however, if the project maintainer finds any NDepend Issues present, your contribution may be edited or sent back to you in order to correct this. For more information, please contact the project maintainer. Code that does not follow code guidelines: DREditor is intended to be used by users who do not code AND people who are new to programming. Therefore, on top of following NDepend rules, programmers must follow Uncle Bobs Guide to Clean Code. This is to enforce 2 goals of DREditor. For more information, you can check out our coding guidelines. : "Programmers should not want to blow their head off reading the code". "Someone who does not know how to code, should be able to reasonably piece together what your code does". AI Generated or Assisted Contributions: AI contributions in any capacity are not accepted by DREditor. People found to have done so should be reported to the project maintainer so that they may be blacklisted. Though keep in mind that it is insanely hard to spot AI coding, and it is common for human made code to be detected as AI. Contributions from people who do not sign the CLA: This is more of just a formality, and to avoid fallout from arguments in which someone may try to remove their contribution regardless of the reason being malicious or not. To sign the CLA, please contact the project maintainer.

docs/contributionpolicy.html.title: Contribution Policy | DREditor API
docs/contributionpolicy.html.summary: Contribution Policy Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson ALERT: The policy is always subject to change by the project maintainer. If your complaints or arguments are brought up about aspects of the policy, we will update the policy to be as precise as possible. "If you're one of those people who say "Because the policy doesn't cover xyz, that means I can/can't do xyz" to which the response will be becoming the reason why a new aspect of the policy is created." You can find the guide used to make these policies here. Policy Introduction We welcome contributions that do not need much work We encourage contributions and while we try do do it, our existing contributors have limited time to mentor or guide new contributors. When a contribution needs changes, existing contributors will usually make any necessary changes themselves rather than working with the original contributor to make the changes. However, we strive to give primary credit to the original contributor whenever possible. We especially encourage contributions that make it easier for new contributors to become productive without direct mentoring, such as documentation, tutorials, refactoring, tests, and similar. Assigning Credit Our overall philosophy of giving credit is: We give credit by name to all tangible contributors. When submitting a contribution, we expect contributors to include accurate information about who contributed to the work. How we give credit: For code contributions: We add a line to the top of the code file as an Author Like: “Author:” or “Original/Edited/Reworked Author:” or if code is completely reworked with permission from the original contributor, it is up to the reworked contributor whether to give credit to the original contributor if the code file does not remotely resemble the original authors work. However not doing so is usually frowned upon. For code documentation for the API: Only pages in bulk can be submitted. You must request which code file(s) you wish to write documentation for. Please keep in mind that there are some scripts in which the code authors would like to do themselves, so your request may be denied. If accepted you'll be credited on the API website or through a Documentation Authors page on the website. By contributing to the API, you agree that the full credit and control of the code is to the authors of the code file. If you're making tutorials: Contact the project maintainer. Credit yourself however you wish and consider being apart of our public Resources. We reserve the right to change how we give credit when following this policy seems detrimental to our project. Some examples of when we may not follow our credit guidelines: Someone requests credit to a name that is obscene or harmful Someone is spamming multiple projects with useless changes We don't want to be associated with the contributor A contributor is not following our code of conduct or otherwise harming our project Specific instructions for contributors who want credit Please make it easy for us to accept and credit your contribution! Here are the steps to take to get the most credit for your work: Agree to the CLA. (Contact the project maintainer to be sent one) Respond to requests for changes within 7-30 days. Cooperate in good faith with our requests for changes. If you do not want to make changes, please tell us as soon as possible. If for some reasons you can’t or won’t make necessary changes to your contribution, we will reject your contribution and take no further action. Correcting mistakes in credit Sometimes we make a mistake in how we give credit. In this project, we will correct any mistakes in how credit is given, usually by updating the list of authors on the website and including the credit within the repository with a commit so it will be present in the next update. Reporting problems with contributions and credit If you notice that this policy has not been followed properly, please contact the project maintainer or dreditortool@gmail.com and include any relevant information. They will review your report and take any action they deem appropriate, including but not limited to updating credit information, warning the person or organization who did not follow the policy, no longer accepting contributions from a particular source, updating the policy, or any other actions deemed necessary. Contributor names From time to time, names change. Our policy for changing names associated with credit for this project is to contact a maintainer/lead and request the change. You may be asked to resign a CLA. Failure to do so will result in your request being denied. Our convention for names associated with contributions is: Names are unique English Alphabet Only We accept any name a contributor is known by as long as a maintainer can verify your connection to the name using your signed CLA.

docs/introduction.html.title: Introduction | DREditor API
docs/introduction.html.summary: Introduction Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson What is DREditor? The Death Row Editor, or DREditor. Is a Package library for the Unity game engine to allow users to make death-game style games without requiring the need to code. The engine is styled for visual novels/murder mystery investigation, the gameplay similarly found in games like Danganronpa, The Zero Escape series, Your Turn To Die, Ace Attourney, etc. Normally suited for Danganronpa fan games or "Fangans" since a majority of the gameplay possible with this engine can appear extremely true to the originals. Should you use DREditor? DREditor is greatly suggested to projects and users who (are): New to unity. New to programming. Want to create a Fangan or death-game narritive that is a game or a video series. It is extremely recommended that you have assets prepared a head of time, and while not required, there are no temporary assets, and you'll have to provide your own (or at least until some are added to the engine). Temporary assets are fine, but you'll find the best use to be with fully completed assets. Be warned though, this engine is not for the faint of heart. There's a LOT that goes into developing games like this. Even though DREditor allows for the increase in production of these kinds of games, they still usually take years in order to produce the necessary assets to complete even a single chapter. DREditor is simply a streamlined process that brings those assets together to create the desired game. If you feel like DREditor may not be right for your project, feel free to check out a list of alternatives.

docs/limitationsandscenarios.html.title: Limitations and Scenarios | DREditor API
docs/limitationsandscenarios.html.summary: Limitations and Scenarios Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson These are things that are never directly mentioned within the engine or a tutorial but is relevant enough information that should be stored somewhere. Limitations Localization is currently not supported for DREditor in regards to multi language support in a single build. There's nothing stopping you from creating a github branch for a specific language, and translate the project to export a different language that way. It is planned to add localization tools to DRE in the future. One of the least flexible UI's in DREditor is the Main Menu. Because of how the system operates, there are 2 menu groups that must be architecturally structured so that the system doesn't break. You can refer to these from the Main Menu Canvas Template. Start Group: The "Press Any Key" Menu Group. While this specific group isn't required it is highly recommended. Title Group: Must contain New Game, and Load Game. With New Game moving to the Menu Group's New Game Option. Load Game moving to the Save/Load UI, which once a file is loaded through the confirmation pop up will move to the Menu Group. Menu Group: Must contain New Game, and Continue. With New Game, either you manually set up the script to start the game on the button, or move to the Difficulty UI. (Which outside of the difficulty's start game button, can be set up how you wish) The Continue Button must be present under the new game button. So the first 2 buttons must always be New Game, and Load Game. Depending on the circumstance, the DRE Button script should be used instead of the regular unity button script. One example of this is the Quit Game button. As when clicking the button using the regular button script, the pop up UI will display but get stuck on the quit button's menu group. Unless you built it yourself, UI templates will not have mouse point and click interactions since the main menus default state is to have the cursor locked. At the current moment, there is no default Free Time Event Minigame for the player to obtain currency, however this may not always be the case in the future. When using chapter select, the active save data is based on chapter select. (Note: RTMM = Return To Main Menu) V3: Load => Ch select => RTMM => Continue => data when file originally loaded. DREditor: Load => Ch select => RTMM => Continue => data of the ch select. Limitation Scenarios If a ValueWithEvent object has been created for the purpose of updating a runtime state, then a script that implements IToTitleScreen should be made/implement OnDestroy() that resets it's value so that it's state does not carry over during RTMM. There might be load inconsistency bugs between exported live builds if aspects from the previous builds dialogue has changed. As an example, if you changed which sprite is displayed in a chapter of a release build. In the new build, the old sprite will likely be shown on an older save file. If DEFAULT UNLOCKED Chapter Select Scene Data does not contain the unlock data for it's own point in time, the displayed unlocked chapter selects for the save file that starts on that scene will not display unlocked chapter selects properly until it unlocks another one of the chapter selections through gameplay. (The exception to this would be prologue daily life as this should be unlocked on the first line, which means the scene data asset doesn't need to add chapter select data.)

docs/logdesignations.html.title: Log Designations | DREditor API
docs/logdesignations.html.summary: Log Designations Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Types In DREditor, there are many logs that will be displayed to the console, this page gives context to some of the logs you'll see as you use the tool. Within the unity console, there are 3 types of logs: Logs, Warnings, and Errors. If any of these are logged by DREditor, the best way to regard each is as follows: Logs: Simple information being reported, like when specific process like dialogue events are taking place etc. Most of this information can be easily dismissed, and just there to give context. Warnings: Same as logs but if there's any information to keep track of, it'll likely be in a warning. Commonly used with ALERTS to the user. Errors: These will only show up in 2 scenarios, the first being that the user has not plugged something in correctly or has not set something up properly, the second being that there is a bug in the engine, and it is almost never the second. Designations You'll notice that DREditor will categorize it's logs through specific keywords. This is based off of the PODs from the game Nier: Automata. PODs are floating droids that assist the characters of the game, giving these designations at every response. I found this to be quite charming, and considering DREditor is to act as an assistant to developers, I've decided to implement these designations. Below is a guide on what each designation means. These are all self explanitory, but just in case! REPORT/ANALYSIS: Information simply being told to the user./Information ALERT/WARNING: Information that majority of the time requires user attention, or to notify the user that something under the hood has occurred. But the game will still continue to play regardless. HYPOTHESIS: Sometimes the system will try to guess what user is trying to achieve. PROPOSAL: Will give suggestions on what the user should do.

docs/ndependchanges.html.title: Disabled/Edited NDepend Issues | DREditor API
docs/ndependchanges.html.summary: Disabled/Edited NDepend Issues Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson NDepend is an expensive piece of developer software I've used during DREditor development to identify architectural issues within the DREditor codebase, however, some of the issues the system noticed came with issues, either by not noticing that a problem was fixed or the rule being enforced to begin with or the restraints being reasonably modified. Below details which NDepend rules DREditor Violates and are ignored for it's development, and the reason behind the decision. Turned OFF ND1001 - API Breaking Changes: Types. Reason: This system is in it's infancy, API breaking changes are inevitable. ND2102 - Avoid defining multiple types in a source file. Reason: The Core DREditor is still unreworked and contains multiple types in a source file. So this rule was disabled to focus on more real and pressing issues in the codebase. ND1207 - Non-static classes should be instantiated or turned to static. Reason: Wouldn't notice that classes WERE being used just through the editor either through runtime or editor runtime. ND2802 - Assemblies Referenced in Multiple Versions Reason: Got this after upgrading the unity version to unity 6 and I couldn't seem to fix it. ND3120 - Software Composition Analysis (SCA) - Security Reason: I updated to the correct newtonsoft json package it asked for on ndepend but it wouldn't update properly after resolving the issue for some reason. EDITED ND1202 - Class Shouldnt Be Too Deep In Inheritance Tree Edit: Removed the equals sign from the where baseClasses.Count() >= 4 query. Reason: After investigating the wikipidea article it links for "Compisition over Inheritence" it literally says that it's not a hard rule or law of coding. Plus considering that 4 has been the actual max across 1400+ scripts, I'd say we can let this one slide.

docs/resources/artassetguide.html.title: Art Asset Guide | DREditor API
docs/resources/artassetguide.html.summary: Art Asset Guide Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson To start, it is highly recommended that all assets on your project have their dimension sizes divisible by 4. This is to prevent bloat in your project in the long run, as unity has a built in compressor that needs asset dimensions divisible by 4. CG's and Fullscreen Assets CG's and Fullscreen assets should be 1920x1080, or whatever the default resolution you plan to have for your project. It is highly recommended though to stay within the 1920x1080 rule though. Videos Videos are usually considered a full screen asset. Videos shouldn't usually have sound since they can usually synced by adding the audio to FMOD and just calling in normally through dialogue. Note that any audio that is left on will still play in the game, however because it is not passed through FMOD, the volume of the audio for the video cannot be changed so at the very least make sure it is not too loud. It should also be noted that if you are wanting a video that contains transparency, it must be exported as a .webm. Additionally .webm also appears to be relatively optimized so webm's are highly suggested. Character Sprites Naming Convention Sprite files should be named appropriately, the best convention being: CharacterFirstName_SpriteCode . Examples of this would look like: Damon_1a or Damon_Happy . This convention is followed for two reasons: Ensures no additional work needs to be done when writing dialogue syntax, and so that the auto character importer can properly set the sprite codes for the characters sprite. Note that while following this convention is not required , be warned that by not doing so you will have to update each sprite's sprite code manually on the character asset. Dimension Size It is HIGHLY recommended that your character sprites be dimensions that are 2048x2048, 1024x1024, 512x512, etc. Note that it must stay consistent throughout ALL characters. Otherwise you will have to do much more extra work. The reason is so characters are scaled relative to each other, so that their heights in-game match their actual heights. Therefore, it is highly recommended to create a height chart so that artists know how to size the characters proportionately to each other. As an example, here is one of the tallest and one of the shortest characters in Project: Eden's Garden, Wolfgang and Toshiko. Notice how there's a bunch of empty space around Toshiko? This is so that when we paste both characters on the same canvas, their heights in the game will always be scaled correctly to each other, no matter what. Otherwise, character sprites should be good to go! Replacing an Imported Sprite Make sure that the new sprite is named THE EXACT SAME AS THE TEMPORARY ONE. Find the sprite you want to replace in your project window. Right Click: Show in Explorer Click and drag your new sprite into the folder that pops up. Your computer will ask you if you want to replace the existing file, confirm this action. Once it's done replacing, you can close the explorer window and go back into unity, it'll recompile, and once it's done, you should see that your sprite has been updated without breaking anything! Nameplates If you are using image nameplates for your characters, the dimensions size doesn't matter so long as: The dimension size is divisible by 4. ALL nameplates dimensions sizes are the same. To make this easier on artists, it is suggested to make the nameplate for the character with the longest name first. Whatever the size to the nearest number divisible by 4 is, that will be the dimension size you use for all nameplates. A suggested dimension size would be 592x84.

docs/resources/jargon.html.title: Jargon | DREditor API
docs/resources/jargon.html.summary: Jargon Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson In DREditor, there are many common terms and phrases used to describe specific systems, functionalities, etc. This page is to compile a glossary of these terms in the event they are not explained in a tutorial or any other do Common Jargon used with DREditor Actuator: Stemming from the definition of a mechanical device that moves or controls or starts something. Actuators are apart of the Trigger system, where they are categorized as the scripts that decide "How a trigger can be activated, or start." . There will only ever be one Actuator per Game Object. Subsequent: The second half of the trigger system, where they are categorized as the scripts that decide "What a Trigger should do once it's been activated." or "The subsequent action after actuation." . There is no limit to the amount of Subsequents per game object. NSD: Non-Stop Debate. Panel (Debate Context): A panel is best understood as a Dialogue line that additionally contains data for phrases. This "Dialogue line" is broken down into pieces at the discretion of the user, these pieces become phrases. Phrase (Debate Context): Phrases are the word or words broken down from panels, each phrase has the ability to have dynamic data applied to it and can then be animated at the discretion of the user. This functionality is the foundation for debate style gameplay. RTMM: Return to Main Menu. TPFD: Two-Point-Five D or (2.5D). Relating to the cardboard cutout style of how rooms can be viewed through DREditor. FTE: Free-Time Event, or time during the gameplay process that can be treated as a "Free-Roaming" mode. Shells (Prefab Context): The base prefab that DREditor Template Prefab Variants are extensions of. The shells contain very little like the hollowed out state of whatever process it holds. This tends to be scripts the template uses that we know will never change. Shells (Room Building Context): The state of a room the game loads in the event that no room state could be loaded matching the objective/point in time the player is currently at. "The default state of a room, usually by chapter." Project Prefab Variant: The name given to a Unity Prefab Variant of a DREditor Template for your specific project. Project prefabs are commonly suffixed with the acronym of the project.

docs/tutorials/actors.html.title: Actors | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/actors.html.summary: Actors Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Assets to Prepare Required Minimum for One Character A correctly formatted Neutral sprite of the character. Suggested Assets to Prepare As many of the finalized versions of your characters sprites. A correctly formatted nameplate of the character. (However, if you are not planning on using image nameplates and instead just text, then you can just leave/remove the field with the transparent image on the actor importer.) It is suggested that you set up at minimum 2-3 characters, so you'll be able to test the flow of dialogue early. Import Nameplate/Texture Note You may notice that after importing your character with their nameplate. It may not show up correctly dimension wise on the UI. Once you've followed the later tutorial that deals with the DREditor Template Structure, once you've made your Dialogue System Prefab for your project, you can go to the nameplate image, assign one of your characters nameplates to the field, and press the Set to Native Size button, this should set the dimensions on the UI to the dimensions of the nameplate. In your root project folder, Right Click > Create > Folder named Art. In your Art folder, Right Click > Create > Folder named UI. In your UI folder, Right Click > Create > Folder named Nameplates. In your nameplates folder you can click and drag all character nameplates into the project window. Ctrl+a to select all In the inspector window, under texture type, you're going to select "Sprite 2D and UI" Under sprite mode, make sure it says "Single" and NOT "Multiple" Click apply. Done! Importing an Actor/Character Project Window: Right Click: Create/Folder name it sprites. For each character you want to import. Inside the sprites folder, create a new folder with the characters first name, Open that folder. Click and drag your sprites into the project window folder. Ctrl+a to select all In the inspector window, under texture type, you're going to select "Sprite 2D and UI" Under sprite mode, make sure it says "Single" and NOT "Multiple" Click apply. Auto Import an Actor/Character Note This process assumes that your currently active scene is your DRE_Dialogue duplicate. Ctrl+a to select all the sprites in your character folder. DREditor/Characters/Auto Setup Character A window will appear. Fill out the characters first and last name. You can pick a color to correspond with the character so that the dialogue asset UI can be color coded. The neutral sprite for your character should be populated, but if it isn't correct, you can assign the Neutral sprite for your character by clicking on the circle to the right of the field. Same process above for the Nameplate. When you're ready, you can click the "Create" button. Make sure that all your characters sprites are selected before pressing the Create button. What the Importer has Done for you Each sprite now has a corresponding material. This is because during dialogue, when a character is focused on it displays the sprite, while in the overworld a material is used in order to support things like lighting effects. An actor object in your hierarchy has been created and filled out for you. You can look at them in the scene view. Created a Character Database if one was not already present in your project. Created and filled out the Character Asset for your character and added it to the Character Database. Filled out each characters material and sprite along with setting the name for the sprite code. Created a Dialogue Asset of that character showcasing the imported sprites. It can be found at Assets/Dialogues/Debugging/Sprites. Assigning a Conversation to an Actor At this point, you should be able to hit the play button and go up to your character and talk to them. It will tell you that there is no conversation present, and to not save your game on the line. We need to give dialogue to the actor so that when we click on them, we can have a conversation. To do this, we can go to our Dialogues folder and find our Debug Sprite Dialogue asset In the Hierarchy, click on your character, In the inspector window, you should see the actor script. There will be a dropdown that says conversations. Hit the plus button. You can now drag your debug sprite dialogue asset into the first dialogue field. Click play and you can now talk to your character! Updating the Actor Body Position You might notice that depending on the true height of your character, the camera position may not be right. So follow this process to set each characters camera body position. In your project window, to the top right, there should be a search bar. Type Actor_Body_Debugger. You should see it show up in your project window, click and drag it into the heirarchy. Click play mode and go talk to one of your characters. Press the v key. use Alt + tab to free your mouse while in play mode. In the hierarchy, go to the character you're speaking to and click the dropdown next to the name. Then click the drop down on Character. You should see the game object Body click it. In the inspector window, under the transform component, you can see the XYZ Position of the body. Click on the number in the Y position and change it's value; or, click on the letter Y and drag horizontally. You should see that the camera's y position is moving. Change the XYZ values for that character until the view is to your liking. Once you've got the position to where you want, in the inspector, Right click on the position label, and select Copy. Press the play button again to leave play mode. In the inspector window, you'll noticed that your values have been reset, so right click on the position label again, and select Paste. ctrl + s to save the changes to the scene. Do this process for each character. Creating your Character Prefab As stated before, a character should now be in your scene once you've imported it. We are going to turn this into a asset so that the game can spawn the character when we go into a room where the character is located. Make sure that in the hierarchy, all of your characters should have no conversations on the actor script, the number to the right should say 0. Go to the root folder in your project window. (Assets Folder) Right Click > Create > a new folder called Prefabs. Inside the Prefabs folder, Right Click > Create > a new folder called Actors. While inside your Actors folder. In your hierarchy window, click and drag the newly made actor gameobject that was imported into the Actors folder. It will ask you whether to make a prefab or variant. Select Prefab Variant. Press F2 or Right Click > Rename. Remove the " Variant" part of the text, so it's only the characters name on the asset. ctrl + s to save your scene. Go back to your root assets folder. Go through the folders: Resources/Characters Click on your character asset. Without scrolling, you should be able to see a field titled Actor Prefab. Click the circle on the right of the field and search for your characters prefab variant you made earlier. Once you double click it, it should display that it's been assigned. ctrl + s to save. Commit to github at this point if you haven't already. You will follow this process for each character you wish to import. Mass Applying your Character Database to Systems in the Scene There are Multiple systems in DREditor that need the character database in order to function. But in order to keep things organized and less stressful for the end user, templates exist in these scenes that are already set up, except for the character database. Now, instead of making you go find all the different objects that need the reference, a tool is available to auto assign the Character Database (as well as other things like the Progression Database) to all systems that need it in the scene. At the top Menu, go to DREditor/Utility/Scriptable Object Assigner Under the Scriptable Objects Dropdown, click the plus button. Fill the field with your Character Database. Click the Assign to All Components in Scenes button.

docs/tutorials/createdoors.html.title: Create a Door | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/createdoors.html.summary: Create a Door Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Create a ThreeD Door In the Hierarchy, Right click: 3D Object/Quad. Name it whatever. Pressing the T key, you can resize it to something resembling a door. Set the game object layer to the Door layer. Add the Door component through the "Add Component" button. Set the "Door Name" Field to the exact same name as the game object. Fill out the gate field with the gate you want the door to lead too. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Setting the From Position on a 3D Door In your 3D scene start up Play mode. Walk over to where your door is. Position your character as if you just came out of the door. Alt + Tab out and go to the menu item: DREditor/Gates/Set Gate From Location The system will set your player position as the position to set the player when coming from that door from another scene. Create a TPFD Door In order for this system to work, you MUST complete the Leave Ask Dialogue Setup Process! In the Hierarchy, Right click: Create Empty. Name it whatever. Set the game object layer to the Door layer. Add the Door component through the "Add Component" button. Set the "Door Name" Field to the exact same name as the game object. Plug in the gate to the area you want to exit to when the player is in the TPFD room and hits the escape key or the R key. Check the "Is TPFD" box on the door component. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Create a Hitbox Door In the Hierarchy, Right click: Create Empty. Name it whatever. Set the game object layer to the Door layer. Add the Door component through the "Add Component" button. Set the "Door Name" Field to the exact same name as the game object. Fill out the gate field with the gate you want the door to lead too. Check the "Is Hitbox" box on the door component. Add A Box Collider component through the "Add Component" button. Edit it to fit your needs. Box Collider Component should have the "Is Trigger" option checked. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Test Moving From One Scene to the Other using Doors In your Dialogue scene in the Hierarchy select your Room_Loading_System Check the "Debug Test On Load" box. You can now test moving from one area to the other in play mode. Lock Data Unlocked Dialogues: The conversation that plays once all the flags have been triggered. Flags: List of strings, copy the names of all the flags that need to be complete in order for the door to unlock. Locked Dialogues: The conversation that plays if all the flags are NOT triggered. Make sure that after you edit this data you overwrite the room save you're setting this data on.

docs/tutorials/creatingscenelist.html.title: Creating your Scene List | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/creatingscenelist.html.summary: Creating your Scene List Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson In order to load into a scene from another, they must be added to a scene list in the build profile, otherwise the game won't load the scene and throw errors. File/Build Profiles Press "Open Scene List" To add a scene, simply open up your scene from the project window, and then press the "Add Open Scenes". Make sure that GYM_Splash is always index 0 Make sure that GYM_MainMenu is always index 1 You can change the indexes by clicking and dragging them in the scene list view.

docs/tutorials/finalgameplaysetups.html.title: Final Gameplay Setups | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/finalgameplaysetups.html.summary: Final Gameplay Setups Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Set up Gates In the room you wish to start your games dialogue in, go to DREditor/Gates/Auto Setup Gate. Scriptable Object Assigner For the Gate Database Set up Progression Create a new Folder in Resources called "Progression" Right Click: Create/DREditor/Progression/Database Right Click: Create/DREditor/Progression/Chapter named "Prologue" Set Save Title, and Title Create Objectives with O0_Dialogue or whatever naming convention you're comfortable with. Create a new flag with whatever naming convention. Plug the Prologue chapter into the progression database. Scriptable Object Assigner For the Progression Database Creating the Tutorial Character Go to where your characters are located in the resources folder. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Characters/Student Name the character "Tutorial" Set the first name to "Tutorial" Add them to the character database. Creating the Leave Ask Dialogue Go to your dialogues folder. Make a new folder called "LeaveAsk" Right Click: Create/DREditor/Dialogues/Dialogue Name the dialogue asset "LeaveAsk". Under the Game_Manager_Template, Select the Leave_Ask_Manager_ETemplate Plug in your LeaveAsk Dialogue into the field. Right Click Game_Manager_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Go to the LeaveAsk dialogue asset, have the first line be spoken by the tutorial, and write "Would you like to leave?" or something close. Press the "Add Choice" button. Write Yes and No for Choice 1 and 2 Respectively. At the very top of the dialogue asset should be a check box that says "Instant Dialogue" make sure it's checked. Setting up your Music Jukebox Go to your resources folder. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Audio/Music Playlist FMOD Under Sound_Manager_FMOD_ETemplate, select Music_Manager_FMOD Assign your Jukebox to the Jukebox field. docs/tutorials/nsdtutorial.html.summary: Non-Stop Debate Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson ALERT: You must have Truth Bullets and a Difficulty State Database made in order to use this functionality! Create your NSD Manager In your project window, in the search bar, look for NSD_Manager_Template Click and Drag it into the hierarchy. Set it's X and Z position to 0 Set it's Y position to 2.01 Right Click NSD_Manager_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Now Right Click: Delete the NSD Manager in the hierarchy. In your project window, go to where your trial scene is. Left Click to select it, then Ctrl + D to duplicate it. Press F2 to rename it GYM_NSD Open up GYM_NSD. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Trials/Minigame Type Name it: Non-Stop Debate Under the "Type Name" field set it to the same name: Non-Stop Debate Set the controls key to: nsd Lock the inspector by clicking the lock icon in the top right of the window. Click on your NSD_Manager Project Prefab Template in the hierarchy. Click the "Select" button. It should have updated your project window, showing you where the Prefab is. Click and drag it into the "Prefab" field in the inspector window. Press the "+" button displayed under the previously mentioned prefab field. In the game object field, click and drag your prefab again. Click on the "No Function" drop down. Hover over "NSDManager" Select "StartMinigame" under the Dynamic ScriptableObject section. You can now add this to an minigame type database. Setting Up Dialogue and NSD Gradients In your project window, go to the folder path: TextMesh Pro/Examples & Extras/Resources/Color Gradient Presets Ctrl + D any of the existing gradients F2 and rename it to: HitText Repeat the last 2 processes twice, naming them: ConsentText and ResponseText Set all their color modes to Vertical Gradient, and set each top and bottom color. HitText: Top: #FEBF2DFF Bottom: #F78C1EFF ConsentText: Top: #14B8FFFF Bottom: #317BFFFF ResponseText: Top: #46CBE6FF Bottom: #FFFFFFFF Hittable Text will not display properly in NSD and in regular dialogue, encapsulating dialogue text with the @ symbol will color it with the HitText Gradient. Ex: @Dialogue Text@ Note: You do not need to use the @ symbol when making NSD Text/Panels. Create the Phrase Preset Database In an organized folder, Right Click: Create/DREditor/Minigames/Phrases/Phrase Preset Database In the inspector window of the newly created asset. In the top right there should be a symbol that looks like dials and sliders. Clicking on it should allow you to select a preset. There should be one available to you, double click it. This should fill out the list of presets. On your NSD Asset Fill in the "Ending Panel Group Dialogue" Field with the END Trial Dialogue asset you've just made. If the player makes it to the end of the conversation, this is the conversation that will play before the NSD restarts. Filling out the NSD Instance After Filling out the debate conversation like you would normal dialogue, we can then edit the details of each panel/line and animate the words being spoken during the debate. But because there is literally so much information surrounding NSD, you can view a Full Showcase video going over almost every single detail that goes into creating an instance of these minigames. Keep and mind that this recording was made many months before DREditor Release during a Dev log. So some things may be slightly different, but a majority should still be relevant. docs/tutorials/startingaprologue.html.summary: Starting a Prologue Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Setting up the Room State Manager Search in the project window for the Room_State_Manager and put it into the scene, make sure it's position is 0,0,0. Right Click Room_State_Manager: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant. Open up your new project prefab variant by selecting "Open" in the top right. Select "Actor" in the hierarchy. Fill out the Character Database field. Ctrl + S to save. Setting up the Starting Dialogue for a Game In the project window search bar, type: DRE_Start_Alone_Scene Click and drag it into your first area. Create a new Folder in your Dialogues folder call it "Prologue" to keep things organized. Create a starting Dialogue with Right Click: Create/DREditor/Dialogues/Dialogue. Ensure that your Dialogue's first line must start with a CG, if you do not have one, feel free to use the black screen. To make a CG Event, you can do so by using the drop down under dialogue events under a dialogue line and select "CGDisplay". To end the CG on another line, simply add a CGDisplay event and don't fill it in. Once you complete your starting dialogue. Fill out the Starting Dialogue Field on the DRE_Start_Alone_Scene. In the inspector, select the "Add Component" button and type "Spawnable" and add that component to the game object. Right Click DRE_Start_Alone_Scene: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Open up your newly made prefab variant. Under the Spawnable Component, to the left there are 3 dots, once clicked, you should see an option that says "Initialize Destroy Call" click it. Ctrl + S to save. Now you can use DRE_Start_Alone_Scene in a Room Save. Building a Room Save On the Room State Manager, if you haven't already, Press the "Initialize Builder" Button. In your project folder, go to where your character prefabs are. You can click and drag them into the scene, place them wherever you like. Click on your character in the hierarchy, in the inspector window, under the Actor Script, there is a drop down called "Conversations". Add a new conversation by hitting the "+" button. Assign the dialogue you want the character to have by filling out the top most dialogue field on the characters conversation. Once you're ready to create your room save, just go to your Room State Manager. Select the objective you want the character and it's conversation to be available at. Click "Create Room Save". Once you've created your room save, you can click the "Clear All" Button. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Overwriting a Room Save (Updating a Room Save) Press the load button on the Room State Manager for the save you want to edit. It should load the room save, simply edit whatever you want changed. Press Overwrite on the Room State Manager. Confirm the Overwrite. Press the "Clear All" button. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Triggering a Progression Flag From Dialogue Click on your dialogue asset and scroll to the very bottom. Click the "Trigger Flag" Button Here you can select what flags you want to set as triggered once the dialogue ends. Rules of Thumb for making Objectives/Progression Per Chapter The first objectives being daily life, and however many flags you need. If you are required to talk to a character in order to leave a room or progress, then it will have it's own progression flag. The investigation objective at minimum must as many flags as there are truth bullets for that chapter + 1 , the +1 being the flag to notify that all truth bullet flags have been completed. The Trial Objective only really needs 1 flag, that being that the trial is completed, which should be triggered on the final trial dialogue asset played in the trial. A Post-Trial Objective that only really needs 1 flag to represent that the post trial (and therefore the chapter) has been completed.

docs/tutorials/template-system.html.title: Template System | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/template-system.html.summary: Template System Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson In order to make things simpler for the user, DREditor has many templates, however not all of them are completely filled out. There are tons of templates that need context for your specific project in order to for those systems to function. Therefore, you'll notice that a lot of names of game objects will say "Template" or "ETemplate" or "Shell" or Neither. Each of these symbolizes what steps need to be taken in order for that template to be usable or for it to function properly. In order to use these templates to our advantage. It is essential that anything with a template suffix should be turned into a prefab variant where you replace the "Template" or "ETemplate" part of the name with the acronym of your project. Detailed below. This is done for multiple reasons, one being organizational purposes, the second being so that the templates in your imported samples folder can be updated and/or replaced. As an example, if a new DREditor Version drops and there's mention of a template change, after updating your project through DREditor/Dependencies/Update Package Wizard you can go to the package manager and click on the package that was updated and there should be a Samples section you can click on, and there should be a button that says "Import" or "Re-Import". This will replace your Templates in your Samples folder, therefore it is a rule of thumb in DREditor to never edit a template otherwise when you reimport your samples , your work may be overwritten! This also applies to animations on the templates! No Suffix If a prefab in DREditor does not have any suffix of "Template" or "ETemplate" then it is usually a system that either does not need setting up, or is already filled out for you by default. That said, if you wish to change anything on these, you should make a Project Prefab Variant of it so that in the future data won't get overwritten. ETemplate Short for "Editable Template", these are templates that just need to be filled out. Simply check the fields on the scripts on the game object that are empty and fill them in, whatever they may be. A majority of the time, it's databases or simple things that may not even need a tutorial for. Template There are likely more Templates or ETemplates inside of this template. They are likely a larger system broken up into smaller systems. Where in order to fully "fill out" the template, all of the other templates inside of the template must be filled out or wired to each other first for the template to be considered "filled". Depending on the circumstance, you may need to unpack a template into the shell, then make it into a Project Prefab Variant in order to use it. (See Below) Shells You'll notice that Templates are Unity Prefab Variants already. Meaning there's an underlying prefab that was built off in order to make the Template. This prefab is referred to as the "Shell". The shells contain very little, like the hollowed out state of whatever process it holds. This tends to be scripts the template uses that we know will never change. Making A Project Prefab Variant A "Project Prefab Variant" is simply the name given to a Unity Prefab Variant of a DREditor Template for your specific project. Project prefabs are commonly suffixed with the acronym of the project. Right click on a template in the hierarchy. DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant, A wizard will pop up. The only field you need to fill out is the Suffix. Simply type the acronym for your project. Example 1: Project: Eden's Garden => EG or PJEG Example 2: Kill/Cure: Beautiful Vice => KC or KCBV Example 3: The Uzujigoku Massacre => TUM If you like your acronym, and you know you won't be changing it in the future. You can check the "Permanently Use Settings" check box and from now on you won't have to type your acronym every single time you want to create a project prefab variant. If for what ever reason you don't want to auto set this, you can just click "Create". At this point the system will have updated the prefab in the hierarchy with your new project prefab variant. When you left click on the object in the hierarchy, in the inspector window to the right, you should see 2 buttons "Select" and "Open". You can click on "Open" and from there you can start working on your prefab and applying changes safely. Unpacking a Template for the Shell. Sometimes, when trying to edit a template, unity may stop you, saying that you can't mess with part of a prefab structure (See below image). This usually means you'll have to unpack a template into it's shell then make your Project Prefab Variant so you can edit what you need to. To do this you can Right Click: Prefab/Unpack. Do NOT press "Unpack Completely! Then, right click again and follow the steps to make your Project Prefab Variant. Now you should be able to open your Project Prefab Variant, and make the edits you want. Templates with Animations If you're wanting to use an animation present on the template and edit it. You can do this if you've already made your prefab variant of the template for your project. Right click on the game object containing the animator component and go to DREditor/Duplicate Insert Animation. This will let you choose an output folder to put your animation, be sure to keep things as organized as you can! Once you've selected your folder, it should duplicate the animation for you to edit it as you see fit, and it should automatically plug in the newly duplicated animator.

docs/tutorials/tpfdscenes.html.title: TPFD Scenes | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/tpfdscenes.html.summary: TPFD Scenes Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Making the Scene & it's Room State Manager Go to your GYM_Dialogue scene in the project window. Ctrl + D Select the duplicate and press F2. Or Right Click: Rename Rename it to GYM_TPFD or really whatever you wish. Double Click to enter the scene. Select the Room State Manager (It currently has data for the dialogue scene) Right Click: Delete In the project window go and find your Project Prefab Variant of the Room State Manager. Click and drag it into the scene. Press the "Initialize Builder" Button Clear the Template Environment In the hierarchy, there should be a game object called "Environment" with a dropdown. Left click on the first game object named "Cube" Hold Shift and then select the bottom most game object named "Cube" this should mass select all of the cubes. Right Click: Delete. This should clear the room to just a simple flat floor. Set up the Arrow Canvas for your Project In the project window, search for Arrow_Canvas_Template Click and drag it into the hierarchy window. On it's dropdown in the hierarchy, it should have all the image components for each arrow. You should only ever need 2 images to fill out this Template, an arrow pointing to the right, and an X symbol. Assign the images to each Arrow and X_Mark's Image components. Right Click Arrow_Canvas_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant You can now drag and drop the newly made template for every TPFD scene you have! Setting up the TPFD Manager DREditor/Gates/Auto Setup Gate Check the Is TPFD box on the gate that was made and showed up in the inspector. In the project window type "TPFD_Manager". Click and Drag it into the hierarchy. Zero out it's position. Ctrl + S to save the scene. Click on your TPFD_Manager in the hierarchy and in the inspector, check the "Debug Mode" box. On your Project Prefab Variant for Room_Loading_System in the scene, hit the drop down and click on the Room_Loader. Check "Debug Load Room On Start". Press the Unity Play Button. Alt + Tab to free your mouse, and click on the TPFD_Manager in the hierarchy. In the inspector window, you can manipulate the camera position and boundaries of the scene in TPFD mode. Adjust them to your liking. Once you're done, DO NOT EXIT PLAY MODE, right click the title of the TPFD Manager script in the inspector window, and copy the component values. Then exit play mode. Right click on the title of the TPFD Manager script. Click "Paste Component Values". Uncheck the "Debug Mode" box. Ctrl + S to save the scene. If you want to leave a TPFD room by pressing Escape or the R key, you must make a TPFD Door.

docs/tutorials/trialstutorial.html.title: Trials | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/trialstutorial.html.summary: Trials Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Initializing Trial Scene Setup Open up your GYM_Trial scene, or whatever you named your trial scene. Mass Select from the Controls_UI_Canvas_ETemplate to the Letter_Box_Canvas Right Click: Delete Menu Item: DREditor/Utility/Scriptable Object Assigner Click the "+" button on the Scriptable Objects list. You're going to fill the field with your Character Database Click "Assign to All Components In Scenes" Go to your GYM_MainMenu scene. Mass Select your Global Systems (Select everything that is NOT from the Build_Version_Canvas to the Fast_Forward_To_Line_Tool) Right Click: Copy Move back to your GYM_Trial scene. Right Click: Paste to the hierarchy. Reorganize things to where global systems are separated from the trial systems. (Click and drag them above the ====ENVIRONMENT==== game object.) Open your Dialogue_System Prefab Ensure that the 3D_UI_Canvas's canvas component is disabled. (Check box next to the script name) Make sure that you add the trial scene to the Build Scene List (File/Build) Setting Up Your Trial Camera Animations In your root project folder, Right Click: Create/Folder called Animations Inside that folder, create another folder called: Trial Camera In your Hierarchy, Left click DRCameraAnchor Right Click DRCameraAnchor: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant In the inspector window, press the "Open" button Right Click DRCamera_Pivot: DREditor/Duplicate Insert Animation Make sure that the target directory field says Assets/Animations/Trial Camera Set the Affix Separator to "None". Click "Duplicate", this will duplicate all the template trial animations. In your project window, Right Click: Create/DREditor/Trials/Camera Anim Database In your project folder you'll find an Asset called "TrialCamera" this is the animator controller for the trial camera. Click and drag that asset into the Trial Camera Animator Controller Field. Click "Import Animation Clips" Setting Up The Trial Dialogue Minigame Manager, TimeUp and Continue_Confirm Dialogues In your Dialogues folder, make a new folder "Trial". Inside that folder, Right Click: Create/DREditor/Dialogues/Trial Dialogue Name it Continue_Confirm Ctrl + D to duplicate it, press F2 to rename the duplicate to TimeUp. Fill out both dialogues with at least one line from your protag for when they refuse to give up after a game over and the line they say when they run out of time in a minigame. In the hierarchy select Trial_Dialogue_Minigame Fill out the continue confirm and time up fields with the dialogues you've just made. Right Click Trial_Dialogue_Minigame_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Press the Open Button In the Hierarchy Search Bar search for Trial_Camera_Animation_Handler There should be 2, select both or one at a time. On both, Fill in the TCAD field with the Trial Camera Anim Database you made in the previous tutorials. Setting Up the Trial Discussion Minigame Type In your Resources folder, make an new Folder named: Trial Right Click: Create/DREditor/Trials/Minigame Type Name it: Trial Discussion Under the "Type Name" field set it to the same name: Trial Discussion Set the controls key to: td Lock the inspector by clicking the lock icon in the top right of the window. Click on your Trial_Dialogue_Minigame Project Prefab Template in the hierarchy. Click the "Select" button. It should have updated your project window, showing you where the Prefab is. Click and drag it into the "Prefab" field in the inspector window. Press the "+" button displayed under the previously mentioned prefab field. In the game object field, click and drag your prefab again. Click on the "No Function" drop down. Hover over "TrialDialogueMinigame" Select "StartMinigame" under the Dynamic ScriptableObject section. You can now add this to an minigame type database. Setting Up a Trial Discussion You can now make Trial Discussion assets, Right Click: Create/DREditor/Dialogues/Trial Discussion and just fill in the fields with Trial Dialogues. The common naming convention for trial discussions is: TD_ChapterNumber_DiscussionNumber with Trial Dialogues named: TD_ChapterNumber_DiscussionNumber_DialogueNumber Setting Up the Trial Minigame Type Database In your Resources/Trials folder. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Trials/Minigame Type Database Add your Trial Discussion minigame type to the databases list. Creating a Trial Builder Asset In an organized folder in the project window. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Trials/Trial Builder Asset Click the "Add a new part of the trial" button. From the dropdown you can select which minigame type you want. Fill the field with the minigame asset for that minigame's type. (Trial Discussion Assets for the Trial Discussion type, etc.) Setting Up Your Trial Manager Prefab Left Click on the Trial_Manager_Template in the hierarchy. Under the Trial Sequencer Script, fill in the trial discussion type with the trial discussion type you made previously. Right Click Trial_Manager_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Under the Trial Manager Script you can now add Trials per chapter. Make sure they are kept in the proper order. (Prologue/Chapter 1 first and so on) Setting Up Your Trial Characters Menu Item: DREditor/Characters/Auto Setup Trial Character Under the Spawn Settings header, look for the "Ignored Characters" list. Add your Tutorial character to this list. The only other option you should ever really mess with is the "Number of Objects" dial to set up how many characters will participate in the trial. (Not Counting Hosts) Use the Dropdowns in the circle UI to set up each characters assigned seats in the trial. Where the top most seat will be in front of the brown host chair in the scene template. When ready, click the "Create" button at the bottom. Ctrl + S to save the scene. To do your hosts, essentially do this same process, but fill the "Ignored Characters" Field with the already created Characters + Tutorial. Once they spawn, you can simply just move the host to where you wish. Post Trial Scene After the results of a trial, what usually happens is a dialogue sequence. So we'll set up the Trial scene as a TPFD (2.5D) scene for the game to transition out of Trial Gameplay. Select your Trial Scene in your project window. Ctrl + D to duplicate it. F2 and rename it to something like: GYM_Trial2D Open it up. Delete everything except for the ====ENVIRONMENT==== game object in the hierarchy. Under the ====ENVIRONMENT==== game object's Character object, delete the Trial Characters present. Click on the ====ENVIRONMENT==== game object under the transform component near "Scale" click on the chain icon. Set the x scale to 1/3 and hit enter. The entire room should now scale down to a smaller size. (The Trial scene is 3x bigger so we're scaling it down.) In your project window, search for your Room State Manager, and Set up the room as you would a TPFD Room. You'll want an On Load Actuator with a dialogue subsequent to start up the post trial dialogue scene. It is suggested that the dialogue ends on a black CG for smoother transition to the end of the chapter. Make sure that you add this scene to the Build Scene List (File/Build) At the bottom of your Trial Builder asset, fill out the field with GYM_Trial2D so that when a trial ends, it moves to that scene. (Or you can fill in the gate field) (Do NOT fill in both) Finishing a Chapter On the final dialogue asset that's played, scroll to the bottom and click "Enter Scene" Write GYM_SavePoint or whatever your Save point scene name is. Open up GYM_SavePoint Make sure that you add this scene to the Build Scene List (File/Build) Open up GYM_Credits Make sure that you add this scene to the Build Scene List (File/Build) Assuming all of the steps have been completed in combination with the details of your project, the gameplay loop should now be complete, and you can export a build of your game.

docs/tutorials/triggers.html.title: Triggers | DREditor API
docs/tutorials/triggers.html.summary: Triggers Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Triggers, are game objects that contain 2 types of scripts. Actuators and Subsequents. Simply put, the Trigger system can be understood as objects used in Room Building that can be best understood as: "If something happens, the do something." As an example, by looking at a trigger game object, you can understand what a trigger does simply by reading what it's individual parts do. Example: Actuator: OnLoadActuator | Subsequents: DialogueSubsequent Read As: "When the room loads, start dialogue." Actuators Stemming from the definition of a mechanical device that moves or controls or starts something, Actuators are categorized as the scripts that decide "How a trigger can be activated, or start." . There will usually only ever be one Actuator per Game Object. OnLoadActuator: Activates the moment the room loads. (You don't need to fill out any info on this script.) OLFlagActuator: Activates the moment the room loads, and specific progression flags are or aren't triggered. (Only fill out "Call if Flags are" and "Flags" with the names of the flags that should match "Call if Flags are" in order for the Actuator to activate.) HitboxActuator: Activates the moment the player enters the hitbox. (The system will add a hitbox for you to manipulate.) Subsequents Subsequent: The second half of the trigger system, where they are categorized as the scripts that decide "What a Trigger should do once it's been activated." or "The subsequent action after actuation." . There is no limit to the amount of Subsequents per game object. DialogueSubsequent: Responds to Activation by: Automatically starting dialogue. LDialogueSubsequent: Responds to Activation by: Automatically starting dialogue depending on local dialogue evaluation. MovePlayerSubsequent: Responds to Activation by: Moving the Player to the position outlined on the subsequent. Creating a Trigger In the hierarchy, Right Click: Create Empty In the inspector window, click the "Add Component" button in the inspector, and then type the names of any of the Actuator scripts mentioned above. Click the "Add Component" button in the inspector, and then type the names of any of the Subsequent scripts mentioned above. Once both scripts have been filled out. The trigger is considered complete, and can be used in combination with Room Building.

docs/tutorials/truthbulletstutorial.html.summary: Truth Bullets Author: Benjamin "Sweden" Jillson Importing Truth Bullets The Syntax for importing a truth bullet with its description is: TruthBulletName //Description TruthBulletName //Description Menu Item: DREditor/Import/Truth Bullets A window will show up, Close it. The system has Automatically made a database. In your project window: Resources/Evidence Menu Item: DREditor/Import/Truth Bullets In the text area, fill out your truth bullets according to the syntax mentioned above. Click Import. All your truth bullets should now be made. Create a Collection of Evidence In your Resources/Evidence folder. Right Click: Create/DREditor/Investigations/Evidence Left click on the newly made asset. In the inspector window, in the most top right, you'll see an unlock icon, click it to turn it to a lock icon. In your project window, mass select the truth bullets you made. Click and drag them into the truth bullets list in the inspector window. Click the lock icon to unlock the inspector window. Click on your evidence database. Click and drag the evidence asset into the list of evidence. Ctrl + S to save as usual. Setting up the Truth Bullet Menu Go to your Pause_Menu_System Project Prefab Variant and open it. If your Pause_Menu_System Prefab has the Prefab Variant icon after opening it, then Right click it: Prefab/Unpack. Right Click Pause_Menu_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Open up your Pause_Menu Project Prefab Variant. If your Pause_Menu Prefab has the Prefab Variant icon after opening it, then Right click it: Prefab/Unpack. Right Click Truth_Bullet_Menu_Canvas_Template: DREditor/Create Project Prefab Variant Left Click it, find the "Back Group" Field. Click and drag Pause_UI_Canvas into it. Open up your Truth_Bullet_Menu_Canvas Project Prefab Variant. Under the Truth Bullet Menu Script fill in the evidence database field with your evidence database asset. Ctrl + S to save the prefab. After doing this, you may need to rewire the Pause Menu Open up your Pause_Menu_System prefab. Drop down your Pause_Menu Left click on your Pause_Menu_System There should be a fields labeled "First Group" and "Pause Visibility" if they are empty, then proceed with these steps, otherwise, you can skip this. Click and drag Pause_UI_Canvas into the First Group Field. Click and drag Pause_UI_Canvas into the Pause Visibility Field. Drop down your Pause_UI_Canvas Drop down Main_Group Click on your Settings_UI_Button, if you see a field saying "None (Menu Group Base)" then proceed with these steps, otherwise, you can skip this. Drop down your System_Menu Click and drag System_UI_Canvas into the previously mentioned field on the Settings_UI_Button. On your System_UI_Canvas if the field labeled "Back Group" is empty, click and drag the Pause_UI_Canvas into the field. Giving the player Truth Bullets On the dialogue asset you want to give the player a truth bullet. Add a new line. Set the speaker to the Tutorial. For the text you can put: ""XYZ" has been added to your truth bullets." Add a new Dialogue Event "Truth Bullet Get" Assign the truth bullet you want to unlock for the player. Mass Applying Conditions to Dialogue Assets. Every dialogue that you have a truth bullet get, you'll want to not only trigger the flag for getting that truth bullet, you'll also want a "Add Condition" on all these dialogues checking to see if all of the truth bullet flags are triggered, and if so, to play a dialogue informing the player that all truth bullets in the area have been found, and to move on to whatever next steps in your story's investigation should take place. Of course, while you'd have to do this for every single dialogue with a truth bullet get, you can mass edit dialogues to apply that condition. Mass select all relevant dialogue assets. Menu Item: DREditor/Dialogues/Mass Edit Dialogues Fill in the information in the wizard, the GUI is the same as if it were on a dialogue asset. When done, simply click the "Apply to Dialogues" button. You should find that your settings have been applied to all selected dialogue assets.
